analysis.one_liner: Cuts power plant emissions of sulfur dioxide, nitrogen oxides, mercury, and carbon dioxide by 2009.
analysis.headline: Backed by 19 cosponsors including two Republicans, the Clean Power Act of 2003 never advanced past its Senate committee referral and died when the 108th Congress ended on January 3, 2005.
analysis.plain_summary: The Clean Power Act of 2003 would have required power plants to sharply cut four pollutants by 2009: sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxides (the causes of acid rain and smog), mercury (a neurotoxin that contaminates fish), and carbon dioxide (the main greenhouse gas). Plants could meet the limits by cleaning up or by buying and selling emission allowances, but the total nationwide pollution could not exceed the caps. A share of the allowances was reserved for household electricity customers, workers laid off by the transition, hard-hit communities, and renewable energy projects. It never received so much as a committee hearing, and it expired when the 108th Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people living downwind of power plants: the bill's caps on mercury, acid rain gases, smog-forming nitrogen oxides, and carbon dioxide would have reduced asthma triggers, mercury in fish and waterways, and acidified lakes and forests, particularly in the Northeast and Appalachia. Households would also have received a share of the emission allowances' value, workers displaced by the cleanup would have gotten retraining and income support, and renewable energy and efficiency businesses would have gained a new revenue stream.

how_it_helps.text: The bill set hard national limits on power plant pollution: by 2009, no more than 2.25 million tons of sulfur dioxide, 1.51 million tons of nitrogen oxides, and 2.05 billion tons of carbon dioxide per year, and by 2008 no more than 5 tons of mercury.

After setting aside shares for transition aid and clean energy, the bill directed the remaining emission allowances' value to electric utility households, distributed based on household size and state consumption — turning a pollution limit into a partial rebate for electricity customers.

It funded transition assistance for workers laid off because of the emissions cuts and for communities hit by disproportionate economic losses, through grants for retraining, income support, and local job attraction.

It required continuous monitoring of plant emissions and ambient air around large coal plants, with results made available to the public, and gave the EPA authority to crack down on any plant causing significant local harm even if it held enough allowances.

It directed federal monitoring and protection of ecosystems damaged by acid rain, including the Adirondack and Appalachian mountains, the Great Lakes, Lake Champlain, Long Island Sound, and the Chesapeake Bay.

analysis.who_pays: Coal-burning power plant owners and, downstream, the coal mining industry and coal-dependent regions, which would have faced the largest compliance costs. Some of those costs would likely have shown up in electricity prices, though the bill returned a large share of allowance value to households and cushioned displaced workers and manufacturers with transition allocations.

drawbacks.text: The bill relied on a cap-and-trade system: plants that found cleaning up expensive could buy allowances from cleaner plants instead, which could leave pollution concentrated around the plants that kept emitting, even as the national total fell.

Power plants would have passed compliance costs to customers, and regions that depend heavily on coal for electricity — and on coal mining for jobs — would have faced the sharpest price and employment effects.

The bill softened the blow for industry itself: through 2018 it handed free allowances to existing power plants and to electricity-intensive manufacturers, meaning some of the value of polluting would keep flowing to the same companies being regulated during the transition.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit side is large: deep cuts in four pollutants with known health and ecological harms, financed partly by giving the allowances' value back to households, workers, and communities rather than only to industry. The costs are real and concentrated — coal-burning utilities and coal mining regions in the Midwest and Appalachia would bear the heaviest burden, and electricity rates could rise where coal dominates. The bill cushioned those costs with free transition allowances through 2018, worker retraining money, and aid to hard-hit communities, and it kept local-impact backstops and studies of trading hotspots. On the whole, the design was a serious, if industry-cushioned, attempt at the emissions problem; its main flaw was dying before anyone could improve or vote on it.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee the day it was introduced, never received a hearing or markup, and expired when the 108th Congress ended.

narrative.text: The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Environment and Public Works on February 12, 2003; no further committee action appears in the record.
A year later, on February 24, 2004, Senator Jeffords delivered introductory remarks on the measure again, but the bill still never advanced.
The bill died when the 108th Congress ended on January 3, 2005, without a committee vote, a floor vote, or any action in the House.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Coal-burning power plant owners and the coal industry were better off, because they avoided mandatory four-pollutant emission limits for at least another Congress. The Bush administration's preferred approach, which covered fewer pollutants, remained the working framework. The public got none of the promised mercury, acid rain, or carbon dioxide reductions.

for.name: Jim Jeffords
for.role: U.S. Senator from Vermont; ranking member, Environment and Public Works
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on it again in February 2004, but could not get it scheduled in committee.

for.name: Olympia Snowe and Susan Collins
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, the only two Republicans among its 19 cosponsors.

against.name: James Inhofe
against.role: Chair, Senate Environment and Public Works Committee
against.what_they_did: Chaired the committee the bill was referred to and never scheduled it for a hearing or markup during the two-year Congress.

against.name: Coal and electric utility interests
against.role: Coal producers and coal-fired power plant owners
against.what_they_did: Fought mandatory power plant emission caps and backed the weaker competing approach.

against.name: Bush administration
against.what_they_did: Promoted the Clear Skies Initiative, a competing bill covering fewer pollutants and omitting carbon dioxide, which gave the Senate majority an alternative and reduced pressure to act on the Jeffords bill.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's sponsorship was bipartisan — an Independent sponsor with 17 Democratic and 2 Republican cosponsors — but the committee that buried it had a Republican chair and majority, and no action was ever scheduled.

industries.note: The bill capped sulfur dioxide, nitrogen oxides, mercury, and — for the first time — carbon dioxide from power plants, forcing owners to install controls, switch fuels, or buy allowances. It cushioned them with free transition allowances through 2018, but the long-run direction was less coal burning. The public cost of these plants' emissions — asthma, mercury in fish, acidified lakes — is what the bill would have reduced.

A binding carbon dioxide cap plus steep sulfur and mercury limits would have cut demand for coal, the fuel most exposed to all four limits. Coal-dependent regions like Appalachia were listed among communities the bill would have compensated, an acknowledgment of where the job losses would fall.

Up to 20 percent of each year's emission allowances would go to wind, solar, biomass, geothermal, efficiency projects, and clean new fossil units — a revenue stream for companies that emit little or nothing. Their gain comes from the same shift that cleans the air, so their interest ran alongside the public's.

Aluminum, chemical, and other electricity-heavy producers would receive a share of allowances to offset higher power costs, protecting them from passing price increases to consumers. This was a targeted cushion, not a windfall.
